q: Which state did the United States buy from Russia in 1867?
fact: The price was 7.2 million dollars - about two cents an acre. Critics mocked the deal as 'Seward's Folly'.

q: What is the national bird of the United States?
fact: It has been on the Great Seal since 1782, but only became the official national bird by law in 2024.

q: Which river carved the Grand Canyon in the United States?
fact: The canyon is about 446 km long and up to 1.8 km deep, cut by the river over millions of years.

q: Which national park in the United States, created in 1872, is widely considered the world's first?
fact: It sits on top of a supervolcano and holds about half of the world's active geysers.

q: Which sport was invented in the United States in 1891 using a soccer ball and two peach baskets?
fact: Its inventor, James Naismith, was a Canadian teacher working in Springfield, Massachusetts.

q: Canada holds the world record for the longest what?
fact: Counting its islands, Canada's coast stretches about 243,000 km - enough to circle the equator six times.

q: What is the official national winter sport of Canada?
fact: Canada also has an official national summer sport: lacrosse, first played by Indigenous peoples.

q: Which animal, an official symbol of Canada, appears on its five-cent coin?
fact: The trade in beaver pelts drove much of Canada's early exploration. The polar bear is on the two-dollar coin.

q: Which dish from Quebec in Canada is made of fries, cheese curds and gravy?
fact: It first appeared in rural Quebec snack bars in the 1950s. Fresh curds should squeak when you bite them.

q: Canada produces most of the world's supply of which sweet product?
fact: The province of Quebec alone makes about 70% of the world's maple syrup and keeps a strategic reserve of it.

q: What is the name of the territory Canada created in 1999 as a homeland for the Inuit?
fact: Nunavut means 'our land' in Inuktitut. It is bigger than Mexico but home to only about 40,000 people.

q: Mexico City was built on the ruins of which Aztec capital?
fact: Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco and was one of the largest cities in the world around 1500.

q: Which holiday in Mexico honors loved ones who have passed away with altars, marigolds and sugar skulls?
fact: Families say the scent of marigolds guides the spirits home on November 1 and 2.

q: What kind of animal is the axolotl, found in the wild only in the lakes of Mexico City?
fact: It keeps its feathery gills all its life and can regrow lost limbs - even parts of its heart and brain.

q: In which part of Mexico do the Maya ruins of Chichen Itza stand?
fact: At the spring and fall equinoxes, the shadows on its main pyramid look like a serpent sliding down the steps.

q: Mexico was the first country to host the men's FIFA World Cup twice. In which years?
fact: Both finals were played in Mexico City's Estadio Azteca - won by Pelé's Brazil in 1970 and Maradona's Argentina in 1986.

q: What is the main ingredient of guacamole, a dip from Mexico?
fact: The name comes from Aztec words meaning 'avocado sauce'. Mexico grows more avocados than any other country.

q: Which martial art from Brazil is disguised as a dance, with acrobatics, music and singing?
fact: It was developed by enslaved Africans in Brazil and is played inside a circle of people called a roda.

q: Which giant statue looks out over Rio de Janeiro in Brazil from Corcovado mountain?
fact: Finished in 1931, the statue is 30 meters tall and its arms stretch 28 meters from hand to hand.

q: What is Brazil named after?
fact: Brazilwood was prized in Europe for its red dye. Its name comes from 'brasa', the Portuguese word for ember.

q: Brazil has been the world's largest producer of which crop for more than 150 years?
fact: Brazil grows roughly a third of all the coffee in the world.

q: Roughly what share of the Amazon rainforest lies inside Brazil?
fact: The rest is spread across eight other countries and territories, with Peru and Colombia holding the next biggest parts.

q: Which music and dance style is the heartbeat of Carnival in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil?
fact: Rio's samba schools spend the whole year preparing floats and costumes for their parade in the Sambadrome.

q: Which dance was born in the port neighborhoods of Buenos Aires, Argentina, in the late 1800s?
fact: Tango also grew up across the river in Montevideo - UNESCO lists it as heritage of both Argentina and Uruguay.

q: What is the highest mountain in Argentina, and in all of the Americas?
fact: At 6,961 meters, Aconcagua is the highest peak in the world outside Asia.

q: The name Argentina comes from the Latin word for which metal?
fact: Early explorers chased rumors of a mountain of silver - which also named the Río de la Plata, the 'River of Silver'.

q: Which city in Argentina is often called the southernmost city in the world?
fact: Ushuaia sits on Tierra del Fuego and is the main departure port for cruises to Antarctica.

q: Which game played on horseback is the official national sport of Argentina?
fact: Pato means 'duck' - early games were played with a live duck in a basket instead of a ball.

q: What is the sun on the flag of Argentina called?
fact: It recalls the May Revolution of 1810, the first step toward independence from Spain.

q: Which desert in northern Chile is the driest non-polar desert on Earth?
fact: Some of its weather stations have never recorded rain, and NASA has tested Mars rovers on its soil.

q: Roughly how long is Chile from north to south?
fact: Yet it averages only about 180 km wide - you can ski in the Andes and reach the Pacific on the same day.

q: Chile is the world's largest producer of which metal?
fact: Chile mines about a quarter of the world's copper, much of it from giant open pits in the Atacama.

q: Which independence leader ruled Chile as Supreme Director from 1817 to 1823 and is honored as its founding father?
fact: His father was an Irishman who rose to become the Spanish viceroy of Peru.

q: Which poet from Chile, author of 'Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair', won the Nobel Prize in 1971?
fact: Chile has two Nobel poets: Gabriela Mistral won in 1945, the first Latin American author to do so.

q: Which Inca citadel high in the Andes of Peru was revealed to the wider world in 1911?
fact: Built around 1450, it was never found by the Spanish conquerors, which is why it survived so well.

q: Which city in Peru was the capital of the Inca Empire?
fact: The Incas called it the 'navel of the world', and their stone walls still line its streets.

q: Which vegetable was first farmed in the Andes of Peru, where thousands of varieties still grow?
fact: Peru has more than 3,000 kinds of potato, in shapes and colors most of the world never sees.

q: In ceviche, the national dish of Peru, what 'cooks' the raw fish?
fact: The acid in lime juice firms up the fish. The leftover marinade is called 'tiger's milk'.

q: Which wild relative of the llama appears on the coat of arms of Peru?
fact: Vicuña wool is among the finest and most expensive in the world - the Incas reserved it for royalty.

q: Whom is Colombia named after?
fact: Columbus never set foot there. The name was first proposed for the whole New World before it stuck to one country.

q: Which author from Colombia wrote 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'?
fact: The 1967 novel, set in the fictional town of Macondo, helped win him the Nobel Prize in 1982.

q: Colombia is world-famous for mining which green gemstone?
fact: Colombian emeralds, especially those from the Muzo mines, are considered the finest in the world.

q: Colombia has more species of which animals than any other country on Earth?
fact: Around 1,900 bird species live in Colombia - nearly one in five of all the bird species on the planet. Peru is a close second.

q: Which singer from Barranquilla, Colombia, performed the 2010 World Cup anthem 'Waka Waka'?
fact: Her full name is Shakira Isabel Mebarak Ripoll - her father's family came from Lebanon.

q: Cuba is the only home of the world's smallest bird. Which is it?
fact: It is only about 6 cm long and weighs around 2 grams - less than a small coin.

q: The streets of Cuba are famous for being full of what, kept running since the 1950s?
fact: New cars were hard to import for decades, so owners became experts at keeping old Chevrolets and Fords alive.

q: Which sport is widely regarded as the national sport of Cuba?
fact: It arrived from the United States in the 1860s. Cuba went on to win Olympic gold in 1992, 1996 and 2004.

q: The name of 'ropa vieja', one of the national dishes of Cuba, translates as what?
fact: The shredded beef stew is said to look like a pile of colorful rags.

q: Which music genre was born in Jamaica in the late 1960s and carried around the world by Bob Marley?
fact: It grew out of ska and rocksteady. UNESCO added reggae to its cultural heritage list in 2018.

q: The team from Jamaica that inspired the film 'Cool Runnings' competed in which Winter Olympic sport?
fact: The team made its debut at the 1988 Games in Calgary, only months after its members first saw a bobsled.

q: Which sprinter from Jamaica ran the 100 meters in a world-record 9.58 seconds in 2009?
fact: Bolt won both the 100 m and 200 m at three Olympic Games in a row - 2008, 2012 and 2016.

q: What is the national fruit of Jamaica, eaten with saltfish in its national dish?
fact: Ackee came from West Africa in the 1700s. Cooked, it looks surprisingly like scrambled eggs.

q: The Blue Mountains of Jamaica are world-famous for growing what?
fact: Grown on cool, misty slopes, Jamaica Blue Mountain is one of the most expensive coffees in the world.

q: Antigua and Barbuda is said to have one beach for every what?
fact: Locals proudly count 365 beaches on the island of Antigua alone.

q: Sir Vivian Richards, from Antigua and Barbuda, is a legend of which sport?
fact: The island's main stadium is named after him. He never lost a Test series as captain of the West Indies.

q: On Big Major Cay in the Bahamas, visitors famously swim with which animals?
fact: Nobody is sure how the pigs reached the uninhabited island - one story says sailors left them there.

q: Roughly how many islands make up the Bahamas, not counting thousands of tiny cays?
fact: Only around 30 of the islands are inhabited.

q: Which pink bird is the national bird of the Bahamas?
fact: Great Inagua island is home to tens of thousands of them - the largest breeding colony of Caribbean flamingos.

q: Which pop star from Barbados was declared a National Hero of the country in 2021?
fact: She was born Robyn Rihanna Fenty in Saint Michael parish, and the street she grew up on is now Rihanna Drive.

q: Which sea creature is served with cou-cou in the national dish of Barbados?
fact: Flying fish can glide above the waves for 50 meters or more, and one appears on the Barbadian dollar coin.

q: Which citrus fruit is believed to have first appeared in Barbados in the 1700s as a natural cross?
fact: It is a cross between the sweet orange and the pomelo, both brought to the Caribbean from Asia.

q: Belize is the only country in Central America with which official language?
fact: Belize was a British colony until 1981, though many Belizeans also speak Kriol, Spanish or Maya languages.

q: What is the Great Blue Hole, off the coast of Belize?
fact: It is over 300 meters across and about 125 meters deep - a cave that flooded when sea levels rose.

q: What is the Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia, the largest of its kind in the world?
fact: After rain, a thin layer of water turns its 10,000 square km into the world's biggest mirror.

q: Although Bolivia has no coast, it still keeps which of these?
fact: The Bolivian Navy patrols Lake Titicaca and the country's big rivers, and marks a 'Day of the Sea' each March.

q: How many official languages does the constitution of Bolivia recognize?
fact: Spanish shares official status with 36 indigenous languages, including Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní.

q: Bolivia is named after which independence leader?
fact: Bolívar was also the country's first president. The city of Sucre is named after his most trusted general.

q: Which phrase, meaning 'pure life', is the everyday greeting and unofficial motto of Costa Rica?
fact: Costa Ricans use it for hello, goodbye, thank you and 'everything is fine'.

q: In most years since 2015, where has more than 90% of Costa Rica's electricity come from?
fact: Rivers, volcanic heat, wind and sun do the work - the power grid has run for months at a time without burning fossil fuels.

q: Which parrot, found only on Dominica, is shown on the country's flag?
fact: Also called the imperial amazon, it is one of the rarest parrots in the world. The flag even uses purple for it.

q: By which nickname is Dominica known?
fact: Rainforest covers most of the island, which has nine volcanoes and is said to have a river for every day of the year.

q: Santo Domingo, in the Dominican Republic, is home to the oldest what in the Americas?
fact: The city was founded in 1496 and also had the first university and the first hospital in the New World.

q: Which sport is the great passion of the Dominican Republic, home of many stars of the US major league?
fact: Around one in ten Major League Baseball players was born in the Dominican Republic - more than in any country except the United States.

q: What is Ecuador named after?
fact: A monument near Quito marks the 'Middle of the World' - though GPS shows the true line is about 240 meters away.

q: Which islands belonging to Ecuador helped inspire Charles Darwin's theory of evolution?
fact: They are named after their giant tortoises - 'galápago' is an old Spanish word for tortoise.

q: The summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth's surface farthest from what?
fact: Earth bulges at the equator, so Chimborazo's peak is about 2 km farther from the core than Everest's.

q: Which thick, stuffed corn flatbread is the national dish of El Salvador?
fact: The country celebrates National Pupusa Day on the second Sunday of November.

q: What does the name El Salvador mean in English?
fact: Spanish conquerors named the territory in honor of Jesus Christ, 'the Savior of the World'.

q: Grenada is called the 'Spice Isle'. Which spice appears on its flag?
fact: Nutmeg trees arrived in 1843 and thrived - Grenada became one of the world's biggest producers.

q: What unusual attraction opened on the seabed off Grenada in 2006?
fact: It was the world's first underwater sculpture park. Corals now grow over its life-size human figures.

q: What is the quetzal, which gives its name to the currency of Guatemala?
fact: Maya rulers wore the resplendent quetzal's long green tail feathers. The bird also appears on the flag.

q: Tikal, in Guatemala, is a ruined city of which ancient civilization?
fact: Its tallest temple rises about 65 meters above the jungle - and appeared as a rebel base in the first Star Wars film.

q: How does the height of Kaieteur Falls in Guyana compare with that of Niagara Falls?
fact: It drops 226 meters in a single plunge and is one of the most powerful waterfalls on Earth.

q: The name Guyana comes from an indigenous word said to mean 'land of many' what?
fact: It fits: the Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice are just three of the country's great rivers.

q: The Demerara region of Guyana gave its name to a well-known type of what?
fact: Demerara sugar's large golden crystals were first shipped from plantations along the Demerara River.

q: In 1804, Haiti became the first country founded after a successful revolt by whom?
fact: Haiti was also the first independent nation in Latin America and the Caribbean.

q: Which two languages are official in Haiti?
fact: Nearly everyone speaks Creole, yet it only gained official status alongside French in 1987.

q: The Citadelle Laferrière in Haiti is often called the largest what in the Americas?
fact: Built on a mountaintop in the early 1800s, its walls rise up to 40 meters and it could hold thousands of soldiers.

q: What does the name Honduras mean in Spanish?
fact: Columbus is said to have named it for the deep waters off its northern coast.

q: The town of Yoro in Honduras holds a festival each year for a legendary 'rain' of what?
fact: After heavy storms, small silver fish are found flopping on the ground. Nobody is quite sure how they get there.

q: The Bay Islands of Honduras lie along the world's second-largest what?
fact: The Mesoamerican Reef runs about 1,000 km from Mexico to Honduras. Only Australia's is larger.

q: Lake Nicaragua is famous for which animals, rarely found in fresh water?
fact: Bull sharks swim up the San Juan River from the Caribbean, jumping its rapids almost like salmon.

q: On the slopes of Cerro Negro in Nicaragua, visitors try which unusual sport?
fact: Riders slide down the black ash of an active volcano on wooden boards, at speeds that can top 80 km/h.

q: In which year did the canal across Panama open to ships?
fact: A French attempt in the 1880s failed. The United States then took ten years to finish the job.

q: What raises ships 26 meters above sea level as they cross Panama through its canal?
fact: The locks lift each ship in three steps and lower it again in three more. A full crossing takes about 8 to 10 hours.

q: Which huge bird of prey is the national bird of Panama?
fact: Its rear talons can be as long as a grizzly bear's claws - strong enough to snatch sloths and monkeys from the trees.

q: What is unusual about the national flag of Paraguay?
wrong: It is taller than it is wide
fact: The front shows the national coat of arms and the back shows the treasury seal with a lion.

q: Besides Spanish, which indigenous language is official in Paraguay and spoken by most of its people?
fact: Paraguay is one of the very few countries in the Americas where most people speak an indigenous language.

q: Despite its name, what is 'sopa paraguaya', a national dish of Paraguay?
fact: Legend says a president's cook added too much corn flour to a soup - and he liked the solid result.

q: The giant Itaipú Dam on the border of Paraguay supplies most of the country's what?
fact: Itaipú, shared with Brazil, is one of the biggest hydroelectric plants in the world. Paraguay sells much of its share.

q: Which founding father of the United States was born on Nevis, in Saint Kitts and Nevis?
fact: Hamilton left the Caribbean as a teenager. His birthplace in Charlestown is now a museum.

q: The scenic railway of Saint Kitts and Nevis was originally built to carry what?
fact: The narrow-gauge line circled Saint Kitts to feed its sugar factory, which closed in 2005.

q: What are the Pitons of Saint Lucia?
fact: Gros Piton and Petit Piton rise straight from the sea to over 700 meters, and inspired the triangles on the flag.

q: Saint Lucia is often said to be the only country in the world named after what?
fact: It honors Saint Lucy of Syracuse - French sailors are said to have landed on her feast day, December 13.

q: Derek Walcott and Arthur Lewis gave Saint Lucia one of the world's highest rates per person of what?
fact: Lewis won for economics in 1979 and Walcott for literature in 1992. Both were born on January 23.

q: Which film series turned Wallilabou Bay on St Vincent into the harbor town of Port Royal?
fact: Parts of the set built for the 2003 film still stand on the bay and can be visited.

q: What is La Soufrière on St Vincent?
fact: It erupted in 2021, covering the island in ash. Its French name means 'sulfur outlet'.

q: Which starchy fruit, brought to St Vincent by Captain Bligh in 1793, is part of its national dish?
fact: Bligh's first attempt to ship breadfruit ended with the famous mutiny on the Bounty.

q: Which language is the official language of Suriname, a legacy of its colonial past?
fact: Suriname was a Dutch colony until 1975. On the street, most people also speak Sranan Tongo.

q: Roughly what share of Suriname is covered by forest - one of the highest figures of any country?
fact: Most of it is untouched Amazon rainforest, while nearly all Surinamese live along the coast.

q: In 1667 the Dutch kept Suriname and, in exchange, let England keep which future American city?
fact: Under the Treaty of Breda, New Amsterdam stayed English. Sugar-rich Suriname looked like the better deal then.

q: Which dance from Trinidad and Tobago has dancers bend backward to pass under a low bar?
fact: The bar is lowered after every round. Limbo began as a ritual performed at wakes on the islands.

q: Pitch Lake in Trinidad and Tobago is the world's largest natural deposit of what?
fact: You can walk on its surface. Its asphalt has paved streets around the world, from New York to London.

q: Which drink do people in Uruguay carry everywhere, sipping it from a gourd through a metal straw?
fact: Uruguayans drink more mate per person than anyone else, often with a thermos tucked under one arm.

q: Uruguay was the first country in the world to give every public primary school student what?
fact: The Plan Ceibal program handed out its first laptops in 2007 and had reached every public primary school by 2009.

q: Angel Falls in Venezuela holds which world record?
fact: Water drops 979 meters from a table-top mountain. The falls are named after Jimmie Angel, a pilot who landed there in 1937.

q: The name Venezuela means 'Little' what, after stilt houses that explorers saw on a lake?
fact: The houses on Lake Maracaibo reminded Amerigo Vespucci's expedition of the Italian city in 1499.

q: Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela has more of what than any other place on Earth?
fact: The Catatumbo lightning flashes on well over 100 nights a year, sometimes for hours on end.

q: Which cornmeal bread, split open and stuffed, is eaten every day in Venezuela?
fact: A favorite filling is the 'reina pepiada' - chicken and avocado, named in honor of a Venezuelan beauty queen.

q: Which is the only country in the Americas where Portuguese is the official language?
fact: A 1494 treaty split the New World between Spain and Portugal, and the eastern bulge of South America fell to Portugal.

q: Which country does Easter Island, famous for its giant moai statues, belong to?
fact: The island lies more than 3,500 km off the mainland. Its people, the Rapa Nui, carved about 900 moai.

q: In which present-day country did Christopher Columbus first land in the Americas in 1492?
fact: He came ashore on an island he named San Salvador, then sailed on to Cuba and Hispaniola.

q: Despite its name, the Panama hat is traditionally woven in which country?
fact: The straw hats were shipped through Panama and worn by canal workers, and the wrong name stuck.

q: Panama was part of which country until it broke away in 1903?
fact: The split came just as plans for the canal were taking shape. Work on it began the following year.

q: Larimar, a rare sky-blue gemstone, is found in only one country in the world. Which?
fact: It is mined in one mountain area near Barahona and was named in 1974 after the finder's daughter Larissa and 'mar', the sea.

q: Which country is the home of mole, a rich sauce made with chili peppers and chocolate?
fact: Mole poblano can contain more than 20 ingredients. The states of Puebla and Oaxaca both claim to be its birthplace.

q: Which country fills its streets with Junkanoo parades on Boxing Day and New Year's Day?
fact: Dancers in huge crepe-paper costumes 'rush' through Nassau before dawn to cowbells, drums and whistles.

q: Which is the only country in the world crossed by both the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn?
fact: The equator crosses the city of Macapá in the north, and the Tropic of Capricorn runs through the north of São Paulo.

q: Allspice, also known as pimento, gives which country's famous jerk seasoning its signature flavor?
fact: The dried berries taste like cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves combined - hence the name. Jerk is traditionally smoked over pimento wood too.

q: Which country in the Americas was the first to declare independence from a European power?
fact: The declaration came in 1776. Haiti followed in 1804, and most of Latin America in the 1810s and 1820s.

q: Which country gave the world both the merengue and the bachata?
fact: UNESCO lists both as cultural heritage - merengue since 2016 and bachata since 2019.

q: The Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland, lies mostly in which country?
fact: It is one of the best places on Earth to see jaguars, giant otters and hyacinth macaws.

q: Which country in the Americas has the largest proven oil reserves?
fact: At around 300 billion barrels, its reserves are the largest of any country in the world, ahead of Saudi Arabia.

q: Which is the largest Spanish-speaking country in the world by area?
fact: It covers about 2.8 million square km and is the eighth-largest country on Earth.

q: In which country's mountain forests do millions of monarch butterflies spend the winter?
fact: Some fly more than 4,000 km from Canada and the northern United States to reach the fir forests of Michoacán.

q: Which country's national soccer team is nicknamed 'La Albiceleste'?
fact: The name means 'the white and sky blue', after the stripes of the team's shirt and the national flag.

q: Cricket great Brian Lara, who once scored 400 not out in a Test match, comes from which country?
fact: His 400 against England in 2004 is still the highest individual score in Test cricket.

q: Which country shares the mighty Iguazu Falls with Brazil?
fact: The falls are made up of about 275 separate drops. The biggest is a U-shaped chasm called the Devil's Throat.

q: Toussaint Louverture is the great national hero of which country?
fact: Born into slavery, he became a brilliant general and led the revolution, but died in 1803, months before independence.

q: The poet and independence leader José Martí is the national hero of which country?
fact: Lines from his 'Simple Verses' are sung all over the world in the song 'Guantanamera'.

q: In which country have Welsh-speaking communities lived in the region of Patagonia since 1865?
fact: Settlers came looking for a place to keep their language alive. Towns such as Gaiman still serve Welsh afternoon tea.

q: In the children's books, which country does Paddington Bear come from?
fact: He arrives in London from 'darkest Peru'. The author first planned Africa, then learned there are no bears there.

q: Winnie-the-Pooh was named after a real black bear called Winnipeg, who came from which country?
fact: A soldier bought the cub in Ontario in 1914 and left her at London Zoo, where Christopher Robin Milne loved to visit her.

q: Which country abolished its army in 1948 and promised the money to schools and health care?
fact: The old army headquarters in the capital, San José, was turned into the National Museum.

q: Which country invented the steelpan, a musical instrument first made from oil drums?
fact: It is often called the only major acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century.

q: Which country hosted and won the very first FIFA World Cup, in 1930?
fact: Only 13 teams took part. The final was played in Montevideo's Estadio Centenario, built for the tournament.

q: Simón Bolívar, 'the Liberator' of much of South America, was born in which country?
fact: He was born in Caracas in 1783 and helped free six present-day countries from Spanish rule.

q: Which country's flag shows a broken trident, standing for its break from colonial rule?
fact: The trident of the sea god Neptune appeared whole on the old colonial badge. Independence snapped off the shaft.

q: Which country's flag carries 27 stars - one for each state and one for the federal district?
fact: The stars show the sky over Rio de Janeiro on November 15, 1889, the day the republic was declared.

q: In which country is rodeo the official national sport, with riders called huasos?
fact: It is ridden in pairs inside a crescent-shaped arena called a medialuna, and became the national sport in 1962.

q: Which country hosted the first Olympic Games ever held in South America, in 2016?
fact: Rio de Janeiro welcomed more than 11,000 athletes. Golf and rugby returned to the Games after decades away.

q: Which country is home to the Arenal volcano and the Monteverde cloud forest?
fact: More than a quarter of the country is protected in national parks and reserves.

q: In which country can you visit the Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá, built 180 meters underground in a salt mine?
fact: Miners first carved a small chapel there. Today's cathedral, opened in 1995, can hold thousands of visitors.

q: Which mountain range, running the length of South America, is the longest on land in the world?
fact: The Andes stretch more than 7,000 km through seven countries, from Venezuela down to the tip of Chile.

q: Roughly what share of all the river water flowing into the world's oceans comes from the Amazon?
fact: The Amazon pours about as much water into the sea as the next seven largest rivers combined.

q: Which of North America's Great Lakes is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area?
fact: It holds enough water to cover all of North and South America to a depth of about 30 cm.

q: Which stormy headland at the southern tip of South America was long feared by sailors?
fact: Before the Panama Canal opened, ships between the Atlantic and the Pacific had to brave its winds and giant waves.

q: The Caribbean Sea takes its name from which people, who lived on its islands before Columbus arrived?
fact: The Caribs, also called Kalinago, still have a territory of their own on the island of Dominica.

q: What is the Darién Gap, between Panama and Colombia?
fact: It is the only break in the Pan-American Highway, which otherwise runs from Alaska to the tip of Argentina.

q: Which bird of the Andes is one of the largest flying birds in the world, with wings over 3 meters across?
fact: Condors can soar for hours without flapping, riding mountain air currents. They appear on several national coats of arms.

q: In the original South American legend, what was 'El Dorado'?
answer: A king covered in gold dust
fact: The Muisca people of Colombia coated a new chief in gold dust and rowed him onto Lake Guatavita. The city came later.

q: Which of these did NOT originally come from the Americas?
fact: Coffee comes from Ethiopia and reached the Americas in the 1700s. Cacao, potatoes and tomatoes went the other way.

q: What are the powerful tropical storms that strike the Caribbean between June and November called?
fact: The word comes from Huracán, a storm god of the Taíno and Maya peoples.

q: In which sport do the English-speaking Caribbean countries play together as one team, the West Indies?
fact: The West Indies won the first two men's Cricket World Cups, in 1975 and 1979.

q: Which tournament, first played in 1916, is the world's oldest continental soccer championship?
fact: The first edition was held in Argentina to mark 100 years of its independence. Uruguay won it.

q: Which crop, first farmed in Mexico about 9,000 years ago, is now the most-produced grain in the world?
fact: Corn was bred from a wild grass called teosinte, whose tiny ears held only a handful of kernels.

q: Why do the flags of Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela all share yellow, blue and red?
wrong: They copied the flag of Spain
fact: From 1819 to 1831 the three were united as Gran Colombia, under a tricolor designed by Francisco de Miranda.
